sources.entry: With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody. (Hyrum's Law)

summary.title: Hyrum's Law
summary.one_liner: With enough users of an API, every observable behavior of a system gets depended on by someone, so implementation details effectively become part of the interface.
takeaways: With many consumers, all observable behaviors of an interface get depended on, whatever the contract promises.
The implicit interface grows gradually, often without consumers noticing, and can come to exactly match the implementation.
Once the implicit interface matches the implementation, the interface has effectively evaporated and any change may break consumer expectations.
Automated testing can reveal these new expectations but cannot remove them; designers should plan for this when evolving systems.
Hyrum's Law is named after Hyrum Wright, who credits Titus Winters with naming and popularizing it.
summary.summary: The page is an essay by Hyrum Wright, drawing on his work on low-level infrastructure migrations in a large, complex system. It explains the gap between an interface (the abstraction consumers use) and its implementation, and how consumers come to rely on undocumented behaviors such as performance and bugs. It connects this to Spolsky's Law of Leaky Abstractions and the "Law of Implicit Interfaces," and describes how the implicit interface can eventually match the implementation. The author notes that Titus Winters named and popularized the concept.
